title: Chapter XXIII

teacherSummary.text: Sir William announces the engagement; Mrs. Bennet is disbelieving and resentful. Jane receives no word from Bingley, and Elizabeth grows more suspicious of Darcy's and the sisters' influence.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXIII,” how does Austen show family uproar? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXIII develops the idea of family uproar. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and tone / mood shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XXIII to complicate the reader's understanding of family uproar. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of family uproar responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of family uproar. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Why is Mrs. Bennet especially bitter about Charlotte's engagement? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include stability, unfeeling, overpowering, luckily, resolving. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “Unwilling as she was to admit an idea so destructive of Jane’s happiness, and so dishonourable to the stability of her lover, she could not prevent its frequently recurring.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: The state or quality of being stable, or firm.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Engagements reshaped family alliances and resentments. Now, why does this chapter matter? Elizabeth's distrust of Darcy deepens—partly earned, partly prejudice. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Tone / mood, Irony.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot characterization, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
